learn.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
learn.headline: Decision models are cheap evaluators; tune their threshold instead of using 0.5
learn.reason: Changes your eval code; the default cutoff often leaves accuracy unused.

card.headline: Cheap scoring models can grade AI answers, but check their cutoff
card.gist: New small models give each AI conversation a score for how likely it failed. Using their default cutoff without checking it can cost you accuracy.
card.picture: It's like your sklearn classifier's probability output with the usual 0.5 cutoff. On some data, a different cutoff catches far more true cases. You tune it on labeled rows, not by habit.
card.why_you: You will build evals soon, and these models are a low-cost way to grade outputs. Your skills with labels, cross-validation and precision-recall apply directly.
card.remember: Tune the cutoff on your own labeled examples before trusting it.
card.term_meaning: The score above which a model's output is called a failure; the default here is 0.50.
card.say_it: When I use a scoring model as an eval, I tune its cutoff against human labels with cross-validation.
card.follow_up_why: Because the default cutoff may not separate failures from passes well on my specific task.
card.reality_check: This is a blog post on hamel.dev, testing 100 labeled traces from one agent; results may differ elsewhere.
card.try_it: Take any sklearn classifier you have and compare F1 at 0.5 against a tuned cutoff, using stratified five-fold cross-validation.

learn.title: Real AI Agent Attacks and What Would Have Stopped Them — Andrey Rybka, Bloomberg
learn.headline: Real agent security breaches and the controls that would have stopped them
learn.reason: Teaches agent tool-call controls: scoped credentials and checking every input and call.

card.headline: A Bloomberg talk walks through real attacks on AI agents
card.gist: AI agents are programs where a model takes actions, like sending email or running code. The talk covers real incidents and the controls that would have stopped each one.
card.picture: Think of giving each ETL job its own narrow access role. A broken job then cannot touch other tables. Dropping a production table still needs a person to approve.
card.why_you: When you build agents in LangGraph, you decide what each tool may do. These incidents show what happens when those limits are missing.
card.remember: Give an agent only the access one task needs.
card.term_meaning: Hidden instructions inside content an agent reads, which make it do something its owner did not intend.
card.say_it: I treat everything an agent reads as hostile, and send each tool call through a fixed rule-based checker.
card.follow_up_why: Because real agents were steered by hidden instructions, such as in an email or in Morse code.
card.reality_check: These are incidents as described by someone from Bloomberg in a conference talk posted on YouTube.
card.try_it: List every tool one of your agents can call, and mark which ones should need human approval.

learn.title: You can now choose 12-hour prompt caching in the API.
learn.headline: OpenAI offers 12-hour prompt caching, with longer cache writes costing more.
learn.reason: Shows the caching trade-off: pay more to write, pay less to reuse. Common interview topic.

card.headline: OpenAI's API can now keep a repeated prompt part for 12 hours
card.gist: Many requests resend the same instructions and tools. OpenAI can store that shared part, and later requests that reuse it pay a lower price, even hours apart.
card.picture: It's like materializing a shared staging table that many queries read from. Building that table costs more once. Later queries that read it cost less.
card.why_you: Agent loops resend the same instructions and tools on every step. Caching that repeated input lowers its price, which shapes agent cost.
card.remember: Repeated prompt parts can be stored and billed at a lower price.
card.term_meaning: The provider stores repeated prompt input, like instructions and tools, and bills reuse at a lower price.
card.say_it: I keep shared instructions and tools identical across requests so they can be billed at the cached price.
card.follow_up_why: Because cached input is priced lower, and the longer option keeps it stored when requests are hours apart.
card.reality_check: This is OpenAI's own announcement; 12-hour cache writes cost 2.5 times the input token price. Trying it needs OpenAI API access.
card.try_it: Take one LangChain prompt you wrote and mark which parts stay identical across every call.

learn.title: Google Open Sources Harness2 for Self Improving AI Agents
learn.headline: Google open-sources Harness2, letting agents improve their own setup
learn.reason: Shows the agent setup (prompts, tools, memory) improving itself; a clear agent idea.

card.headline: Google open-sources a tool that lets AI agents improve their own setup
card.gist: Everything around an AI model, like its instructions, tools and memory, is its setup. Google's new open tool lets the agent improve that setup for each task, without changing the model.
card.picture: Think of an ETL job that tries a few versions of its own setup. It keeps the version that performs better and saves notes. The next job starts from those notes, not from scratch.
card.why_you: It shows an agent can get better by changing its setup, not the model. That split helps you explain how agents improve.
card.remember: An agent's setup can improve while the model stays the same.
card.term_meaning: Everything around the model: system prompt, tools, memory, skills and subagents.
card.say_it: A harness is the prompt, tools and memory around a model; Harness2 lets the agent refine it per task.
card.follow_up_why: Because a person usually designs the harness once, and that fixed setup is reused for every task.
card.reality_check: Results come from a Reddit post describing Google's tests; the code is open source on GitHub.
card.try_it: Write down the harness of one agent you use: its prompt, tools and memory.
